His emblem is considered `la più vaga (impresa); la più ingegnosa; la più allusiva; e la più perfetta che fino a quel giorno fosse mai stata da veruno nostro accademico esposta` (Memorie ritratti imprese degli Accademici Gelati p. 338). The description of the emblem is in Jacopo Gelli, Divise-Motti e Imprese di famiglie e personaggi italiani (Milano 1928) p. 200.
On Coradino`s authorship of verses in honour of Pope Urban VIII, see Gianluigi Betti, `Un componimento poetico per l`elezione a papa di Urbano VIII nell`accademia bolognese dei Gelati (1623)`, in Il Carrobbio, 28 (2002) pp. 79-92.

022-000000113.Notes: He published poems under the nickname he had in the Selvaggi Academy, see Orlandi Notizie degli scrittori bolognesi 1714 p.143. Motto and emblem are explained in Memorie ritratti imprese degli accademici Gelati, p. 277v. Capponi was part of the Instabili Academy, founded by his uncle Pellegrino, where Giovanni`s emblem was a wool-winder, the motto `Fermo nel piede son se ben m`aggiro`. Giovanni founded the Academia dei Selvaggi in the house of Filippo Certani where his emblem was a bird moving his wings in order to get out of the nest, with the motto `Manca la forza`, and his nickname was Animoso. He played a part in devising the tournament `Amore prigioniero in Delo` (1628), organised by Accademici Torbidi. On Capponi`s biography, see Gian Luigi Betti, `Giovanni Capponi, filosofo, astrologo e politico del Seicento`, in Studi secenteschi (1986)

He was member of the Accademia dei Nobili in Padua. In the Incogniti Academy, Costantini delivered two orations (which remained in manuscript) on Vergil`s Georgiche. 022-000001783.Notes: The pupil of Justus Lipsius at Louvain, Segeth went to Padua in 1597, where he was the guest of Giovan Vincenzo Pinelli. In Pinelli`s house, he befriended Galileo, who gave him a copy of his `Sidereus nuncius` to be delivered to Kepler. Segeth joined the Ricovrati in 1600. In the Academy, he delivered a speech in Latin in front of all academicians, on the subject of man`s aim in life. Apparently, his pronunciation was not so clear, however everybody praised his rhetorical skills.

022-000002263.Notes: Carriero received obtained a degree in canon and civil law in the University of Padua, but he was rather inclined towards literary studies. At the age of 27 he was among the founders of the Animosi Academy. In this context, he delivered two orations, one on dreams, `De somniis deque divinatione per somnia brevis consideratio`, later published in Padua; the other, `Possint ne arte simplicia veraque metalla gigni`, also published later, was about the nature of metals and the way they could be transformed. See his biography by Sandra Olivieri Secchi in DBI.

022-000002492.Notes: Poet. The brother of Francesco Maria Sforza, Bishop of Conversano, Muzio moved to Venice in 1584. His portrait is taken from Delle rime del signor Muzio Sforza parte terza (Venice: Salicato, 1590). Luigi Russo, Muzio Sforza poeta monopolitano tra Rinascenza e Controriforma (Bari: Puglia Grafica Sud, 1985), affirms that he joined the Accademia degli Uranici. His names is also associated to the Accademia Olimpica, see Maddalena Campiglia, Flori, A Pastoral Drama. A bilingual edition, ed. Virginia Cox and Lisa Sampson, transl. Virginia Cox (Chicago: The University of Chicago Press, 2004), p. 321 n.84.

022-000005553.Notes: Criminal and civil lawyer in Venice, historian and writer of music drama, Beregan was also member of the Concordi Academy (Ravenna). He was banned from Venice on 18 February 1656 (1655 according to the Venetian calendar), following the accusation of killing on his gondola a Flemish merchant. Beregan returned to Venice in 1660, without this having any consequences on his life. He joined the Gelati in 1671. See his biography by Giorgio Ferrari, in DBI.

022-000006221.Notes: A letter of his from Padua, addressed to Camillo Vizzani in Rome, dated 22 July 1566, is in the Ranuzzi MSS Ph 12670 at the Harry Ransom Center. The letter mentions Scipione Gonzaga and two Academies, presumably the Eterei Academy in Padua, and the Oziosi academy in Bologna, to which all three apparently belonged: `... non restero` di dargli di V. S. quella notizia che io debbo, et pigliero` fra l`altre occasione dell`Accademia nostra, essendone egli protettore...`. Varoli wishes that when Gonzaga will be in Bologna `... gli fosse fatto dalla nostra Academia una sessione pubblica nella quale si dicessero le sue lode et se gli facesse dono della Academia...` In particular, Varoli asks Vezzani whether he would be willing to use for such occasion a canzone he had previously composed.

022-000006439.Notes: Bon was famous as a numismatist and obtained a degree in civil and canon law in Padua. He joined the Ricovrati in 1678, and was also fellow of the Royal Society in London. In Italy he was also member of the Dodonei (Venice), and Sventati (Udine).

022-000006440.Notes: Canon of the cathedral in Padua, Bombardini joined the Ricovrati in 1683, he became secretary in 1688-89, and in 1692. In Padua he was professor of canon law from 1691, and subsequently of criminal law until 1721. In 1684 Bombardini deleivered a presentation in the Academy: `Chi apportasse maggior utile all`impero romano, o Antonio Pio con la clemenza, o Alessandro Severo con il rigore`. He contributed with a sonnet to Compositioni ... Ricovrati per la morte ... Helena Cornaro Piscopia (1684).

022-000008138.Notes: Liceti was professor of philosophy in the Universites of Pisa (since 1600) and Padua (1609-38). In Padua he also taught theoretical medicine (1645-57). He engaged in polemical exchanges with Galilei, in particular on the problem of moon light. It is in this context that Galileo wrote `Lettera al principe Leopoldo di Toscana`. Liceti was `consigliere` and `censore alle stampe` in the Ricovrati Academy, which he joined in 1619. See his biography by Giuseppe Ongaro, in DBI.

022-000008581.Notes: Joined the Ricovrati in 1689. On the 16th of June 1691, there was a public meeting which was attended by several women, including Lucrezia Capello Gradenigo, the spouse of the `podesta` `, Maria Zorzi Loredana, and several other women from Padua and from aborad. In this context, Obizzi delivered the following oration: `Se fusse piu` lodevole il costume d`escluder le donne dal governo come i Romani, o pure d`ammetterle come i Germani`. Apparently, the topic raised a heated debate. Marco Andrea Zambelli agreed with the first point, while Matteo Forzadura stood for the second option. A couple of years later, in the public meeting which took place in Mantova Benavides family garden, Obizzi had a conversation with Vitaliano Mussato on the following problem: se porti piu` vantaggio nel cuor delle donne a chi le serve il sofferir le loro amorose ingiurie o il rissentirsene.
